column2: Thus addressed, the righteous, self-controlled one with his brothers fell into deep dejection and said nothing.
After reflecting a moment, Yudhishthira, son of Dharma, wretched and given to anxiety and grief, said to his mother:

What is this you have resolved? You should not speak so. I do not give you leave; you should show favour.
mahabharata:15:22.20	Earlier you roused us, pleasing one, with Vidura's words; you should not abandon us.
mahabharata:15:22.21	Having slain the kings I gained this kingdom, hearing your counsel through Vasudeva, bull among men.
mahabharata:15:22.22	Where is that understanding of yours I heard, that you, having spoken of standing in kshatriya dharma, now wish to waver from it?
mahabharata:15:22.23	Abandoning us, the kingdom and these renowned daughters-in-law, how will you live in empty forests? Be gracious to me, mother.
Hearing the tearful words of Kunti's son, she went on, her eyes full of tears; and Bhima said to her:

Kunti, when this kingdom won by your son is to be enjoyed and the duties of kingship gained, how has this thought of yours come?
mahabharata:15:22.26	Why were we made by you earlier to bring about the earth's destruction? For what reason, giving us up, do you wish to go to the forest?
mahabharata:15:22.27	Why were we, children, brought from the forest by you, and these two sons of Madri, overcome by grief and sorrow?
mahabharata:15:22.28	Be gracious, mother, do not go to the forest today, renowned one; enjoy Yudhishthira's fortune won by Partha's strength.
Resolved, she, intent on forest life, did not heed the sons' words as they lamented in many ways.
Draupadi, her face dejected, followed her mother-in-law as she went to the forest, weeping with Subhadra.
She, the greatly wise, looking again and again at her weeping sons, went on, resolved on the forest.
The Pandavas followed her, with servants and the women's quarters; then, wiping her tears, she said to her sons:
When your kingdom was taken at the dice and you had fallen from happiness and been despised by kinsmen, I roused you.
How may Pandu's line not perish, bulls among men? How may your fame not perish? So I roused you.
You are all like Indra, with valour like the gods; do not look to others' faces: thus I did that.
How may the king, best of those who uphold dharma, like Vasava, not be again unhappy in the forest? So I roused you.
This Bhima, with the strength of ten thousand elephants, famed in valour and manliness, must not go to excess: so I roused you.
This younger brother of Bhimasena, like Vasava, Vijaya, must not sink: so I roused you.
These two, Nakula and Sahadeva, devoted to elders, how may they not suffer hunger? So I roused you.
And this tall dark one, glorious, long-eyed, must not be troubled in vain in the assembly hall: so I did that.
The Kurus were dejected, and my father-in-law and the rest, as she, wishing a protector, wailed like an osprey.
When she was seized by the hair by the sinful, ruined-minded Duhshasana, then I was bewildered, king.
For the increase of your radiance I roused you then, with Vidura's words; know that, my sons.
How may this royal line not perish, having got sons of mine from Pandu? So, son, I roused you.
A king who has no son or grandson does not gain the worlds of his good deeds, since his line perishes.
My husband earlier enjoyed the fruit of kingship, sons, gave great gifts and drank soma by rule.
I did not urge Vasudeva for my own fruit; by those words of Vidura's it was done for the rescue.
I do not desire the fruit of kingship, son, won by my son; I desire the holy worlds of my husband by austerity, lord.
Having served my mother-in-law and father-in-law living in the forest, I shall wither my body by austerity, Yudhishthira.
Turn back, best of the Kurus, with Bhimasena and the rest; set your mind on dharma, and let your mind be great."
Then there was a great sound from all of them, O Bharata, as the women of the household wept, seeing Kunti gone so.
Then the Pandavas circled the king to the right, saluted him, and turned back, not having turned Pritha back.
Then the great king Dhritarashtra, Ambika's son, having addressed and restrained Gandhari and Vidura, said:

Let Yudhishthira's mother, the goddess, be turned back rightly; all that Yudhishthira said is surely true.
mahabharata:15:24.6	Having cast aside this great and greatly fruitful lordship of her sons, who would go to the hard forest, leaving her sons like a fool?
mahabharata:15:24.7	She has practised austerity while in the kingdom, given gifts and kept vows; she can do so here today; and hear my word.
mahabharata:15:24.8	Gandhari, I am pleased with the daughter-in-law's service; therefore, knower of dharma, you should give her leave.
So told, Subala's daughter told Kunti all the king's words and her own, specially.
When all the Pandavas had turned back and all the women's quarters, the greatly wise King Dhritarashtra went to the forest then.
The Pandavas, wretched, given to sorrow and grief, entered the city with the women in vehicles.
The city of Hastinapura, with women, aged and children, became as if joyless, silent, its festivity gone.
All the Pandavas were spiritless, filled with anger, bereft of Kunti and very grieved, like calves left behind.
Dhritarashtra, having gone a great distance that day, the lord made his dwelling on the bank of the Bhagirathi.
The fires were kindled rightly by Veda-masters, and shone with best of the twice-born, ascetics, here and there; and that aged king had his fire kindled.
That king, having attended the fires and offered by rule, then worshipped the thousand-rayed sun as it reached evening, O Bharata.
Vidura and Sanjaya made a bed of kusha grass for the Kuru hero, not far from Gandhari.
Near Gandhari, Yudhishthira's mother Kunti, firm in good vows, sat down on the kusha grass.
Vidura and the others sat within hearing of them, and the priests and the twice-born followers as appointed.
Their night, with the best of brahmins reciting and the fires kindled, was like the night of Brahma, increasing joy.
Then, when the night had passed, having done their forenoon rites and offered to the fire by rule, they all set out in order, facing north, fasting.
That first day's stay was very painful for them, grieving and grieved for by the townspeople and country people.
There brahmins who lived in the realm waited on him, and many hosts of kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, bull of the Bharatas.
Surrounded by them, the king welcomed them with talk and, honoured by rule, gave leave to them with their pupils.
In the evening that king went to the Ganga and did purification by rule, and so did the renowned Gandhari.
So others too separately, bathing in the tirthas, O Bharata, Vidura and the other men did all the rites there.
Then Kunti, daughter of Kuntibhoja, brought the aged father-in-law who had done purification and Gandhari to the bank of the Ganga, O king.
The priests made an altar and covering for the king there, and the king, true to his word, offered into the fire there.
Then from the bank of the Bhagirathi he went to Kurukshetra, the learned king with followers, restrained and with senses controlled.
Going there to the hermitage, the wise king reached the royal sage Shatayupa, the wise.
With him the king then went to Vyasa's hermitage, and there he received the upholder of the Kurus by rule, O king.
Receiving the consecration there, the delight of the Kurus then made his dwelling in Shatayupa's hermitage.
The greatly wise king told him the whole rule of forest life, O great king, with Vyasa's consent.
So the great-minded King Dhritarashtra joined himself and his followers to austerity.
So too the goddess Gandhari, dressed in bark and deer-skin, with Kunti, great king, kept the same vows.
By deed, mind, word and eye, king, restraining the host of senses, they took up supreme austerity.
The king, skin and bones, his flesh dried up, matted-haired, in deer-skin, his limbs covered in bark, practised fierce austerity like a great sage, free of faults.
And Kshatta, best in understanding of dharma and wealth, with Sanjaya waited on the king with his wife, himself practising terrible austerity, self-conquered, then thin, wearing bark.
Dvaipayana with his pupils, other perfected sages, and the aged royal sage Shatayupa, supremely righteous,
Kunti, great king, honoured them by rule, and those ascetics were pleased with her service.
There those great sages told tales of dharma, dear one, delighting the great soul, King Dhritarashtra.
In a pause in the talk, the divine sage Narada, who had seen everything directly, told this tale.
Long ago there was a king, like Prajapati, fearless, called Sahasrachitya, Shatayupa's grandfather.
Having placed the kingdom on his eldest son, supremely righteous, the righteous King Sahasrachitya entered the forest.
Having gone to the far shore of blazing austerity, that great-minded king attained Purandara's abode.
King, I have often seen him as I flew in Mahendra's abode, the king whose sins were burned by austerity.
So there was a king named Prishadhra, like the thunderbolt-bearer, who also gained heaven's back by austerity.
In this very forest, king, Purukutsa, son of Mandhata, gained great perfection.
His wife was Narmada, best of rivers; that king, having practised austerity in this forest, went to heaven.
There was a king named Shashaloma, supremely righteous; he too, having practised austerity in this forest, gained heaven.
By Dvaipayana's grace you too, king, having reached this ascetic forest, will go to the hard-to-reach, supreme perfection.
You too, tiger among kings, at the end of austerity, surrounded by glory, will go with Gandhari to the goal of those great souls.
Pandu, always remembering you, near the slayer of Bala, will join you always to the good, lord of the earth.
By your service and Gandhari's, your renowned daughter-in-law Kunti will reach her husband's world.
Yudhishthira's mother, for she is eternal dharma; we see this with divine eye, king.
Vidura will enter the great soul Yudhishthira, and Sanjaya, purified by meditating on you, will reach heaven.
Hearing this, the great soul, the lord of the Kurus, pleased, with his wife, accepted Narada's word, praising him, and paid Narada incomparable honour.
So all the hosts of brahmins honoured Narada greatly, O king, and again and again were glad then out of love for King Dhritarashtra.
[Yudhishthira] "Ah, the blessed one has increased the faith of the Kuru king, and of all these people, and of me, greatly radiant one.
I have something to ask; hear it as I say it, divine sage honoured by the world, about King Dhritarashtra.
You know the truth of all events, joined with divine sight; you see, divine sage, the varied destinies of men.
You have told of the kings' sharing Mahendra's world; but the worlds of this king have not been told, great sage.
I wish to hear from you, lord, this lord of the earth's station, of what kind and when; tell me, who ask."
Thus addressed, Narada, of divine sight and great austerity, spoke these words in the midst of the good, in harmony with all minds.

By chance going to Shakra's hall, I saw Shakra, husband of Shachi, and there King Pandu, royal sage.
mahabharata:15:27.9	There this tale of Dhritarashtra arose, king, about this hard austerity which this king practises; there I heard Shakra say this, king:
mahabharata:15:27.12	'In a car going at will, adorned with divine ornaments, the greatly fortunate son of a sage, his sins burned by austerity,
mahabharata:15:27.13	will move at will through the worlds of gods, gandharvas and rakshasas': that is what you ask me, righteous one.
mahabharata:15:27.14	This great divine secret I have told you with love; for you are rich in learning and your sins are burned by austerity.
Hearing that sweet word of the divine sage, all were glad in mind, and that king too.
So the wise ones, having waited on Dhritarashtra with tales, went where they wished, to the goal of the perfected.
So all the townspeople, grieving, remained about the king, and the brahmins there told tales about the king.

How does that aged king live in a lonely forest, and the greatly fortunate Gandhari and Kunti, Pritha?
mahabharata:15:28.4	The royal sage, who deserved comfort, finds that great forest no comfort. In what state has he reached it, with sons slain and wisdom for eyes?
mahabharata:15:28.5	Kunti has done a very hard thing, not seeing her sons: giving up royal fortune, she chose forest life.
mahabharata:15:28.6	In what state is Vidura, the self-possessed servant of his brother, and the wise son of Gavalgana, who guards his master's food?
Down to the children, those townspeople, struck by anxiety and grief, told such tales here and there, meeting one another.
And all the Pandavas, greatly given to sorrow, grieving for their aged mother, did not stay long in the city.
So too for their aged father, the lord of men with sons slain, the greatly fortunate Gandhari and the greatly wise Vidura.
Thinking of the king, they came to great disgust and remembered again and again the terrible slaughter of kin,
and the destruction of the boy Abhimanyu at the head of battle, and of the mighty-armed Karna who never fled from war.
Remembering likewise the slaying of Draupadi's sons and other friends too, those heroes were not very glad in mind.
Always thinking of the earth with her heroes slain and jewels lost, Bharata, they found no sleep.
Draupadi, her sons slain, and the lovely Subhadra, the two goddesses, were not very glad then, but joyless.
Seeing the son of Virata's daughter, your father Parikshit, they kept their lives, those forefathers of yours.
Those who had always been engaged in royal tasks did no royal tasks then anywhere in the city.
As if possessed by grief, they welcomed nothing; even when spoken to, they did not honour anything in return.
Those heroes, hard to assail, like the ocean in depth, their understanding struck by grief, seemed to have lost their senses.
Then those delights of the Kurus remembered their mother: "How does Pritha, thin, serve the aged pair now?
And how does that king, his sons slain, without support, live alone with his wife in a forest frequented by beasts of prey?
And that goddess, the greatly fortunate Gandhari, her kin slain, how does she follow her blind aged husband in a lonely forest?"
As they spoke so, eagerness arose in them then, and their mind turned to going, from wish to see Dhritarashtra.
Sahadeva, bowing to the king, said this: "Ah, what I have seen of you is going to my heart.
By good fortune I shall see that Kunti, practising austerity, matted-haired, an aged ascetic, scratched by kusha and kasha grass,
brought up in palaces and mansions, who had great comfort; when shall I see my tired, greatly grieved mother?
Impermanent indeed are the courses of mortals, bull of the Bharatas, since the king's daughter Kunti lives unhappy in the forest."
Hearing Sahadeva's words, Draupadi, best of women, honoured and welcomed the king and said:

When shall I see that goddess Pritha, if she is alive? Her living will bring us joy today, lord of men.
mahabharata:15:29.16	Let this be your constant thought, and may your mind delight in dharma, king of kings, you who today will join us to good.
mahabharata:15:29.17	Know, king, that this circle of daughters-in-law stands on tiptoe, longing to see Kunti, Gandhari and father-in-law.
So told by the Panchala queen, bull of the Bharatas, the king summoned all the army chiefs and said this:
Set out my army with many chariots and elephants; I shall see King Dhritarashtra living in the forest.
And the king said to the women's overseers: "Let my various vehicles be made ready, and thousands of palanquins.
Let carts, market-stalls, treasury workers and guards of the treasury go to the hermitage at Kurukshetra.
And whoever among the townspeople wishes to see the king, uncovered, well arranged, let him go, well protected.
Let cooks and kitchen-heads and all the kitchen and varied foods and drinks be carried in carts for me.
Let the departure be proclaimed for tomorrow, without delay, and let various houses be made on the road today."
Having so commanded, the Pandava king with his brothers set out the next day, with women and children in front.
Outside for days, looking after the flood of people, the king stayed five days and then went toward the forest.
Yoke, yoke! with great delight a great sound arose from the cavalrymen shouting there, "Yoke, yoke!"
Some men went in vehicles, some on horses swift as thought, in chariots like cities, like blazing fires,
others on lords of elephants, some on camels, king, and others on foot, fighting with nails and spears.
Townspeople and country people in many kinds of vehicles followed the king of the Kurus out of wish to see Dhritarashtra.
And by the king's word the army chief, the teacher Gautama Kripa, taking the army, went toward the hermitage.
Then the glorious king of the Kurus, Yudhishthira, surrounded by brahmins, praised by many bards, minstrels and panegyrists,
with a white umbrella held over his head, with a great chariot-force, the delight of the Kurus set out.
The terrible-acting Vrikodara, son of the Wind, went with mountain-like elephants furnished with engines and weapons.
Madri's two sons, well surrounded by cavalry, went too, delighting, armoured and banner-bearing.
And the greatly radiant Arjuna followed the king in a chariot like the sun, yoked with divine white horses.
Draupadi and the groups of women, in palanquins, with their overseers, went scattering endless wealth.
That Pandava army, rich in men, elephants and horses, resounding with flutes and lutes, shone then, bull of the Bharatas.
On pleasant riverbanks and by streams, lord of the people, making camps, the bulls of the Kurus went by stages.
The greatly radiant Yuyutsu and the priest Dhaumya guarded the city by Yudhishthira's word.
Then King Yudhishthira reached Kurukshetra, having crossed in order the supremely holy river Yamuna.
He saw from afar the hermitage of that wise royal sage Shatayupa and Dhritarashtra, Kaurava.
Then all the people, delighted, entered that forest at once, filling it with great shouts, bull of the Bharatas.
All the townspeople and those who lived in the realm and the women of the foremost Kurus followed then on foot.
Then the Pandavas went to Dhritarashtra's hermitage, empty, crowded with herds of deer and adorned with plantain groves.
Then ascetics of varied vows gathered there, curious to see the Pandavas who had come.
The king asked them, his throat filled with tears, "Where is our elder father, upholder of the Kaurava line, gone?"
They said to him, "Lord, he has gone to the Yamuna for flowers and a pitcher of water."
By the way they showed, they then went on, and not far away saw them all, on foot.
Then, eager to see their father, they went quickly; and Sahadeva ran with speed to where Pritha was.
The wise one, weeping aloud, touching his mother's feet, and she, her face dim with tears, saw her dear son.
Next Pritha saw the king, Bhimasena, Arjuna and Nakula and hastened to them.
She went before that couple whose sons were slain, leading them; seeing her, they fell to the ground.
The great-minded wise king, knowing them by voice and touch, consoled them, the lord.
Then, shedding tears, they waited on the king with Gandhari and on their mother, by rule.
The Pandavas themselves took water-pitchers from them all, and, with consciousness regained, were comforted again by their mother.
Then the women of the lions among men, the warriors, townspeople and country people saw that king.
King Yudhishthira told that people their names and clans, and the king honoured them in return.
Surrounded by them, his eyes dim with tears of joy, the king thought himself back in Gajasahvaya.
Saluted by the daughters-in-law led by Krishna, the wise king, with Gandhari and Kunti, rejoiced.
Then he came to the hermitage, served by perfected ones and charanas, crowded with those who wished to see him, like the sky with hosts of stars.
With greatly fortunate ascetics who had come from various lands to see the sons of the Kuru lord, the broad-chested Pandavas.
They said, "We wish to know which here is Yudhishthira, and Bhima, Arjuna and the twins, and the renowned Draupadi."
Then the charioteer Sanjaya told them all by name, and Draupadi and all the other Kuru women.

This one, pure gold-fair as the Jambunada, with a body like a great grown lion, with a high nose, broad long eyes and coppery face, is the king of the Kurus.
mahabharata:15:32.6	This one who walks like a mad lord of elephants, fair as pure heated gold, with broad and long shoulders and long arms, is Vrikodara; look, look at him.
mahabharata:15:32.7	This one at his side with the great bow, dark, young, like the leader of an elephant herd, with lion-high shoulders and a gait like an elephant at play, lotus-eyed, is the hero Arjuna.
mahabharata:15:32.8	Near Kunti are the two best of men, these twins, like Vishnu and Mahendra; in the whole world of men there is none equal to them in beauty, strength or conduct.
mahabharata:15:32.9	And this one, lotus-petal-eyed, middle-aged somewhat, blue-lotus-hued, like the city's goddess, standing is Krishna, as if Lakshmi embodied.
mahabharata:15:32.10	At her side the one of best golden hue, like embodied Gauri, standing in the middle, is the best of brahmin women, the sister of the incomparable discus-bearer.
mahabharata:15:32.11	This is the sister of the leader of the king's army, of the colour of a heap of blue lotuses, who always vied with Krishna: she is the chief wife of Vrikodara.
mahabharata:15:32.12	And this, daughter of the king of Magadha, called Jarasandha, is held the wife of the younger son of Madri, fair like a champaka garland.
mahabharata:15:32.13	The one with a body dark as the indivara, standing not near on the ground, is held the wife of Madri's elder son, lotus-eyed.
mahabharata:15:32.14	This one, fair as heated gold, with her son, is the daughter of King Virata, wife of Abhimanyu who was slain in battle, chariotless, by Drona and the others in chariots.
mahabharata:15:32.15	These with partings and hair, in white upper garments, are the king's wives, hundreds of them, the daughters-in-law of this aged king, without heroes, their sons lost, without protectors.
mahabharata:15:32.16	These have been named to you in order of chief, with the uprightness of brahmin-nature, of honest mind and goodness; they were all asked by you, and are pure-souled wives of kings.
So that king, best of the aged Kurus, met those sons of kings and asked all of them about their welfare, when all the ascetics had gone.
And as the warriors set up their camp around the hermitage and put down their loads, he asked about well-being of women, aged and children, as was fit.

And those who live on you, are they too well, your ministers, servants and elders, lord?
mahabharata:15:33.3	Do you follow the way of life of the townspeople served by royal sages? Is your treasury filled without cutting off heirs?
mahabharata:15:33.4	Do you behave suitably to enemies, neutrals and friends, and honour brahmins with grants, as is fit?
mahabharata:15:33.5	Are enemies, elders, townspeople, servants and your own people satisfied with your conduct, best of the Bharatas?
mahabharata:15:33.6	Do you, king of kings, sacrifice with faith to the ancestors and gods, and honour guests with food and drink, Bharata?
mahabharata:15:33.7	And in your realm are the brahmins devoted to their own work, and the kshatriya, vaishya and shudra householders?
Having said this, Dhananjaya said to Daruka: "I wish to see the ministers of the Vrishni heroes, without delay."
By one who lived in lordship and knew the Sankhya and yoga, awakened in more than one system, having seen by divine sight.
